title: House Robber
description: Brute force to optimized: recursive exploration of rob/skip choices versus two rolling variables.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array nums representing money stashed in houses along a street, where robbing two ADJACENT houses triggers an alarm, return the maximum amount of money that can be robbed without ever robbing two adjacent houses.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums array"],["Output","Maximum sum achievable with no two chosen elements adjacent"],["Goal","At each house, choose the better of skipping it or robbing it (its value plus the best from two houses back)"],["Constraints","Up to 100 houses"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"No two adjacent elements can both be chosen, maximize the sum\"","A classic 1D DP: the best answer up to house i is the better of skipping house i (keep the previous best) or robbing it (its value plus the best up to house i-2)"]]}

blocks.text: At every house, there are exactly two choices: skip it (carrying forward the best total achievable using houses before it) or rob it (adding its value to the best total achievable using houses BEFORE its immediate neighbor, since that neighbor cannot also be robbed). The better of these two choices at each house builds up the final answer.

blocks.title: Analogy: Picking Non-Adjacent Seats at a Theater to Maximize Total Ticket Value
blocks.text: Picture choosing seats along a single row to maximize total value, but no two chosen seats can be next to each other. At each seat, the best total achievable is either skipping it (keeping the best total from seats before it) or taking it (its value plus the best total from seats two positions back, since the immediate neighbor is now off limits).

blocks.caption: At each house: best of skipping it, or robbing it plus the best from two houses back

blocks.text: Maximum = 4 (rob houses with values 1 and 3, at positions 0 and 2).
Maximum = 12 (rob houses with values 2, 9, and 1, at positions 0, 2, and 4).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Define best(i) as the maximum achievable using only the first i houses.

Observation 2: At house i, either it is SKIPPED (best(i) = best(i-1)), or it is ROBBED (best(i) = nums[i] + best(i-2), since house i-1 must then be skipped).

Observation 3: best(i) is simply the LARGER of these two choices.

Observation 4: Since only the two immediately preceding best values are ever needed, two rolling variables suffice instead of a full array.
This leads to two rolling variables tracking the best totals up to the two previous houses, updated as the array is scanned left to right.
Recursively try both choices (rob or skip) at every house, without memoization, exploring every valid combination.
Why the code is written this way

items: Trying both choices recursively directly implements the definition.
This recomputes the same positions repeatedly across different branches, costing exponential time; two rolling variables reuse previously computed results directly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 raised to n) without memoization.
Space: O(n) recursion depth.
Limitation: two rolling variables, updated left to right, compute the same answer using only O(1) extra space and O(n) time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain two rolling variables, prev (the best total up to two houses back) and curr (the best total up to one house back), both starting at 0. For each house value n in nums, compute the new best as max(curr, prev + n) (skip versus rob), then shift: prev becomes the old curr, curr becomes the new best. After processing all houses, curr holds the final answer.
Use two rolling variables, updating them left to right as the array is scanned.

Since the best total up to house i depends only on the best totals up to houses i-1 and i-2, maintaining exactly those two rolling values and updating them left to right correctly reconstructs the answer at every position, with the final curr value after processing all houses holding the maximum achievable total.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Recursive, try both choices, no memoization","O(2^n)","O(n) recursion depth","Correct, but exponential."],["Two rolling variables","O(n)","O(1) extra","The expected, efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: House Robber is the foundational "no two adjacent elements" 1D DP problem, directly analogous in structure to the Fibonacci rolling-variable technique.

items: Forgetting that robbing house i requires skipping house i-1 (using best up to i-2, not i-1) in the "take" branch.
Using an unnecessary full DP array when two rolling variables suffice.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "at each house, compare skipping it against robbing it plus the best from two houses back" clarifies the recurrence directly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "maximize a sum with no two adjacent elements chosen", think: 1D DP comparing skip versus take at each position, using rolling variables.

items: How would this change if the houses were arranged in a CIRCLE (the first and last house are also considered adjacent)?
House Robber II (circular version) and Min Cost Climbing Stairs, both closely related 1D DP problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unmemoized recursive approach costs O(2^n); the rolling-variable approach costs O(n), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: 1D dynamic programming with rolling variables, comparing "skip" versus "take" at each position.
Time: O(2^n) for the brute force, O(n) for the DP approach.
Space: O(n) recursion depth for the brute force, O(1) extra for the DP approach.
Most Important Observation: robbing a house forces skipping its immediate neighbor, using the best total from two positions back.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy to medium 1D DP problem.
One line memory trick: skip or take plus two-back, keep the larger.
